Convince
kon-VINSS
verb
From the Latin convincere, “to overcome, to refute, to prove guilty” (con- intensive + vincere, “to conquer”); hence to convict, to prove wrong, to overcome by argument. The modern narrowing to “persuade of a truth” loses the note of guilt; the KJV means to convict.

Biblical Definition

To convince, in the Authorized Version, is to convict — to overcome by argument, to refute, to prove a man wrong and guilty. The Latin is convincere, to conquer utterly; and the KJV’s convince keeps the sterner edge that our softer “persuade” has lost. To convince a man is not merely to bring him round to your opinion, but to overpower his defence and leave him without answer — often to prove him a sinner. So the Lord Jesus flings the challenge, “Which of you convinceth me of sin?” (Joh 8:46) — which of you can prove Me guilty of one? None could. When the accusers of the adulteress heard His word, they “being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one” (Joh 8:9) — the same conquering work, done inwardly by conscience. James says the respecter of persons is “convinced of the law as transgressors” (Jas 2:9) — proven guilty, condemned by the very law he thought to keep. And the elder must be able “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — not to charm them but to stop their mouths, to refute the contradiction and lay the error bare. Here is a word the church needs back. The office of the Word is not only to comfort but to convict; the Spirit is come to reprove the world of sin. Before a man is persuaded of the gospel he must first be convinced of his guilt — conquered, silenced, shut up under sin — that he may flee to the Christ whom none could convince of any.

Webster 1828 Definition

To convict; to refute; to prove wrong or guilty; to overcome by argument — not merely to persuade.

CONVINCE, to convict; to refute; to prove guilty; to overpower by argument.

From Latin convincere, “to overcome, to refute.”

The KJV keeps the note of guilt the modern “persuade” has lost.

Christ asks, “Which of you convinceth me of sin?” (Joh 8:46).

The elder must be able to convince the gainsayers (Tit 1:9).

Key Scripture

Joh 8:46 — "Which of you convinceth me of sin? And if I say the truth, why do ye not believe me?"

Tit 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

Jas 2:9 — "But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors."

Joh 8:9 — "And they which heard it, being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last: and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst."

Modern Corruption

An old word for convicting; it recovers the Word’s work of proving men guilty and shutting their mouths.

expand to see more

The drift here has softened a hard and necessary word. In modern speech to convince a man is simply to bring him to agree — a matter of persuasion, of winning him over, with no thought of guilt. The KJV’s convince is a verdict, not a preference: to convince is to convict, to refute, to prove a man wrong and leave him without a plea. When Christ says, “Which of you convinceth me of sin?” He is not asking who disagrees with Him but who can prove Him guilty. To read the mild modern sense into these texts is to lose the courtroom in them, and to imagine the gospel merely woos the mind when in fact it first arraigns the conscience.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is conviction of sin. The Spirit is come to reprove — to convince — the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment; and no man is savingly persuaded of Christ who has not first been convinced of his guilt. The accusers of the adulteress were convicted by their own conscience and went out one by one; the respecter of persons is convinced of the law as a transgressor; the gainsayer is to be convinced by sound doctrine and his mouth stopped. A ministry that only comforts and never convicts has kept half the Word’s office and lost the sharper half. Grace does not flatter the sinner into heaven; it convinces him of sin, that he may flee to the sinless One whom none could convince of any.
